name: Galium

project_scope.note: Genus lesson only; native-range states unchanged.

shared_genus_recognition.look_here_first: Count the leaflike units at a mature stem node, then inspect stem-edge prickles and flowering shoot length.
traits: Small herbaceous Rubiaceae with four-angled stems and apparent whorls of leaflike organs; two units are enlarged stipules.
Tiny four-lobed flowers and paired one-seeded dry mericarps.
All three may have hooked fruit bristles; fruit hooks alone do not identify G. aparine.
shared_genus_recognition.plain_language: These slender bedstraws look like they have rings of leaves. In fact two are true opposite leaves and the others are leaflike stipules; inspect the stem's tiny hairs and where the flowers branch from the leaf axils.
shared_genus_recognition.family_bridge: Rubiaceae commonly has opposite leaves with stipules; Galium's stipules are enlarged and create apparent whorls.

species_comparison_matrix.Galium virgatum: 1–2 flowers close to node, later short leafy cyme

species_comparison_matrix.photo_role: Three-way burr macro; mark shared trait

field_steps: Count several mid-stem whorls: 6–8 plus retrorse stem hooks suggests G. aparine; four suggests G. texense or G. virgatum.
For four-unit whorls, compare ovate broad blades and longer cymes (texense) versus narrow blades, pale underside structures and short node-bound flowers (virgatum).
Check flowers and mature fruit with a millimeter scale; stop at Galium sp. when characters disagree.
overlap_cautions: Fruit hooks are shared, not an exclusive cleavers character.
G. texense and G. virgatum fruit sizes overlap; use several characters.
Mature whorl counts and stem armature are more reliable than habit or flower color.
Leaflike stipules must not all be labeled true leaves.
This is not a county-native certification or a species-install action.

local_source_pool_lookalikes.difference: Look for a persistent toothed calyx and funnel-shaped corolla, unlike the tiny rotate Galium flower.
Opposite leaves and distinct stipules, not Galium's apparent multi-membered whorls.
Woody shrub with spherical flower heads rather than weak-stemmed herb with axillary cymes.

look_here_first: LOOK HERE FIRST — count leaflike units at three mature mid-stem nodes, then photograph a stem ridge under side lighting. Six or eight apparent units plus backward-pointing hooks favors G. aparine. Four units lead to G. texense versus G. virgatum: compare measured blade width, leaf underside and the distance from node to first flower. Confirm with mature fruits and flower size; stop at Galium sp. when the characters disagree.

anatomy_lessons.title: 1 · Count an apparent whorl
anatomy_lessons.plain: The ring around a stem is not made entirely of true leaves; enlarged stipules look like additional blades.
anatomy_lessons.look_here: Photograph a mature middle node from directly above with a numbered ring and a millimeter scale.
anatomy_lessons.why_it_matters: Six or eight apparent units favor G. aparine; four lead to G. texense or G. virgatum.
anatomy_lessons.photo_role: three-species matched mid-node whorls, true leaf/stipule labels after verification

anatomy_lessons.title: 2 · Read the stem's tiny hooks
anatomy_lessons.plain: A retrorse prickle points backward toward the plant base; a straight bristle does not hook in the same way.
anatomy_lessons.look_here: Side-light the square stem ridge at 10–20× and mark the shoot tip direction.
anatomy_lessons.why_it_matters: G. aparine has backward hooks; G. texense and G. virgatum are described with straighter/shorter bristles.
anatomy_lessons.photo_role: matched stem-ridge macros with scale and stem-tip direction

anatomy_lessons.title: 3 · Turn a leaf over
anatomy_lessons.plain: Abaxial means the lower leaf surface. Compare the raised midrib and any pale tiny blisterlike bumps.
anatomy_lessons.look_here: Photograph upper and lower surfaces of mature blades flat against a millimeter grid.
anatomy_lessons.why_it_matters: G. texense is broader and ovate; G. virgatum is narrow and may show pale raised underside structures; these need voucher confirmation.
anatomy_lessons.photo_role: paired G. texense/G. virgatum leaf blades and abaxial 20× details

anatomy_lessons.title: 4 · Follow the flower stalk
anatomy_lessons.plain: A cyme is a small branched flower cluster. A mericarp is one of the paired fruit halves.
anatomy_lessons.look_here: Show a complete node-to-flower stalk and a mature paired fruit beside a millimeter scale.
anatomy_lessons.why_it_matters: G. texense has longer axillary cymes; G. virgatum flowers can sit close to the node. All three may have hooked fruit, so fruit hooks alone do not diagnose G. aparine.
anatomy_lessons.photo_role: matched flowering nodes plus ripe paired mericarps

comparison_cards.title: Cleavers versus four-whorled bedstraws
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Count 6–8 versus 4 apparent units at mature nodes; check stem-hook direction.
comparison_cards.separator: G. aparine generally has 6 or 8 units and retrorse hooks; the other two have four units.
comparison_cards.caution: Whorl number varies with node position; sample several middle nodes.

comparison_cards.title: Texas bedstraw versus slender bedstraw
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Compare mature blade width, underside texture and flower stalk from axil.
comparison_cards.separator: G. texense typically has broader ovate blades (to about 8.5 × 4.5 mm) and longer several-flowered cymes; G. virgatum has narrower blades (about 2–8 × 0.8–2 mm) and short node-bound flowers.
comparison_cards.caution: Fruit size overlaps; pale underside structures in G. virgatum need authoritative specimen review.

comparison_cards.title: Bedstraw versus field madder
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Inspect persistent calyx teeth and corolla shape.
comparison_cards.separator: Sherardia has a conspicuous persistent toothed calyx and funnel-shaped corolla; Galium flowers are tiny and rotate.
comparison_cards.caution: Compare mature flowers and fruits, not apparent leaf whorls alone.
